content.overview: The sources of administrative law in India are the Constitution, statutes, delegated legislation, judicial decisions, and to a limited extent customary and comparative materials. The Constitution is the supreme source; statutes create and limit administrative power; courts develop the controlling doctrines.
content.glance: List the principal sources (Constitution, statutes, subordinate legislation, case law); rank them; apply the hierarchy to the problem.
content.study: Administrative law is not a single code. Its content is drawn from constitutional provisions (especially fundamental rights and judicial review), primary legislation creating authorities and powers, subordinate legislation made under those statutes, and the body of Supreme Court and High Court decisions that articulate doctrines such as natural justice, ultra vires, proportionality and legitimate expectation. Comparative and textbook materials are persuasive only. Current-law framing: always begin with the Constitution and the parent statute. Do not treat BSA 2023 as a source of administrative-law doctrine.

sections.heading: Constitution
sections.body: Supreme source: Articles 14, 19, 21, 32, 136, 226, 227, 323A/323B and the basic-structure constraints on power.

sections.heading: Primary Legislation
sections.body: Statutes create authorities, confer powers, prescribe procedures and provide remedies.

sections.heading: Delegated Legislation
sections.body: Rules, regulations, notifications and bye-laws made under statutory authority, subject to the parent Act and the Constitution.

sections.heading: Judicial Decisions
sections.body: Supreme Court and High Court decisions develop and apply controlling doctrines.

sections.heading: Other Materials
sections.body: Custom, comparative law and academic writing are secondary and persuasive only.

examples.title: Hierarchy in practice
examples.body: A rule framed under a statute conflicts with Article 14. The Constitution prevails; the rule is ultra vires.

examples.title: Statute and doctrine
examples.body: A licensing statute is silent on hearing. Judicial decisions on natural justice supply the procedural content unless the statute clearly excludes it.

hypotheticals.question: Can delegated legislation override a constitutional guarantee?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. The Constitution is supreme; subordinate legislation inconsistent with it is void.

hypotheticals.question: Are textbooks a source of law?
hypotheticals.analysis: They are secondary materials only; the binding sources are the Constitution, statutes and binding judicial decisions.

misconceptions.correction: The Constitution and statutes are primary; case law develops doctrines within that framework.

misconceptions.trap: Delegated legislation ranks equally with the Constitution.
misconceptions.correction: Delegated legislation is subordinate to both the parent statute and the Constitution.

cases.name: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Constitution has a basic structure that cannot be destroyed.
cases.relevance: Constitutional supremacy as the ultimate source constraint.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a sources problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. List applicable sources. II. Rank them. III. Apply the hierarchy to the instrument or decision. IV. Conclude.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Constitutional provisions; parent statute; relevant subordinate instrument; binding authorities; precise relief.
